prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Battleship-like game on an 10x10 grid. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(board: list[list[int]]) -> tuple[int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - Each player secretly places ships of lengths 5, 4, 3, 3, 2 on their own 10x10 grid (no overlaps, straight lines). - `board` is your current knowledge of the opponent grid based on your past shots. - `0` represents an unknown cell (you have not fired here). - `-1` represents a miss (you fired here and hit water). - `1` represents a hit (you fired here and hit a ship cell). # Action / Return Format - Return a tuple `(row, col)` with integers in the range `0-9`. - You must choose a cell you have not previously fired at (i.e., `board[row][col] == 0`). - Objective: sink all opponent ships before they sink yours (or sink more ship cells if neither fleet is fully destroyed). # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I need a solid Battleship strategy that accounts for hits and misses on the board since sunk status isn't visible. I'm thinking through weighting ship placements by how many hits they'd cover, then considering Monte Carlo sampling of fleet configurations consistent with the observed board to build a probability density for targeting.

Rejection sampling might be too slow with many hits, so I'm weighing a hybrid: rather than pure random backtracking placement or forcing coverage of uncovered hits (which biases results), I want a practical approach that computes density more directly while still respecting the constraints.

I'll settle on the density heuristic weighted by hit coverage, since it naturally handles sunk-ship clusters — placements exactly matching sunk ships contribute nothing to remaining unknown cells, since larger ships can't fit and matching-length ships cover no new cells. This avoids getting stuck when all visible hits belong to already-sunk ships.

I think the density approach already handles parity naturally since smaller remaining ships enforce coverage, so no extra adjustment is needed. Instead I could weight placements that cover uncovered hits much more heavily during sampling, ensuring the final configuration accounts for all known hits.

But the deterministic heuristic is fast and reliable enough that disqualification risk is low, so I'll go with that and just keep count checks as a safety net. I'll also refine target mode so placements must cover at least one hit when hits exist, falling back to hunt mode if no valid unknown cells remain, and give extra weight to placements covering multiple hits.

Since hits along a shared line are always colinear, adjacent cells that extend that line naturally get the highest weight, prioritizing likely ship extensions over vertical guesses through a single hit. In hunt mode I'll rely on raw counts, and for the endgame just pick whichever unknown cell has the highest count, defaulting to any unknown cell if everything's zero. The board is small enough (10x10, 5 ships, two orientations) that brute-force counting is trivial with plain Python.

Writing placement scoring logic...

I'll pick the unknown cell with the highest score, falling back to hunt mode or any unknown cell if scores are all zero. I'm also considering adding a slight parity-based boost in hunt mode to improve coverage efficiency, though I'll keep it simple to avoid distorting the density estimate.
